title.value: Application of Parallel Programming to Reservoir Simulation

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: The finite-difference techniques used in reservoir simulation result in many independent calculations, which are amenable to parallel execution. Applications of vectorization and parallel tasking to simulation using supercomputers have been widely reported. In comparison to the extensive literature on reservoir simulation using supercomputers, there is less literature on reservoir simulation using small parallel computers with manual parallelizing capabilities. This study concerns applying parallel programming to reservoir simulation using a 32-Mbyte, 12-processor parallel computer. The effects of types of table look-ups, number of processes, granularity, load balancing and program structure were studied. Vectorization studies using a minisupercomputer was performed for comparison. Parallelism in a simulator is limited by the time-stepping approach of the finite-difference method. The Laplace transform was applied to the simulation of a one-dimensional oil-water model with the aim of reducing nonlinearities and increasing the time step size. Since parallel execution could be performed during each time step, an increase in the time step size would increase the areas that were suitable for parallel execution. The model simulated was a two-dimensional, two-phase, black oil model with a fully-implicit formulation. Three sizes of models were investigated: 10x10, 15x15 and 20x20 grid-block reservoirs. The differenced equations were solved by the Newton-Raphson method, and Gaussian elimination was used to solve the Jacobian matrix. The simulator was parallelized using monitors as macros to synchronize calculations. The time-consuming parts of the calculations were matrix generation and matrix solution, and these parts were parallelized. The performance of the simulator was measured by the speed up, which is defined as the ratio of the sequential execution time of the simulator to the multiprocessing execution time of the simulator. The speed ups of the matrix generation time increased almost linearly with an increasing number of processes. The speed ups ranged from 3.5 to 4.0 for four processes and 7.0 to 7.9 for eight processes. For a 15x15 grid-block model, the parallelized Gaussian elimination resulted in speed ups of 2.8 for four processes and 3.9 for eight processes. The low values were largely due to the small granularity of the procedure, and hence caused large synchronization time. The advantage was the simplicity in programming Gaussian elimination, thus permitting a study of the overall parallelization of a simulator without major reprogramming. An overall speed up of 5.99 was expected if Barua's (1989) matrix solver were to have been used. In the investigations on the application of the Laplace transform to simulation, a modified IMPES equation was discretized with respect to space. Subsequently, the resulting equation was transformed with respect to time. The pressures and saturations of the model behaved more linearly in the transformed space than in the real time space. Nonetheless, the time step size did not show improvement in Laplace space. A favorable result of this study was that, during breakthrough, the transform method needed fewer iterations than the real time simulation. For example, for the maximum stable time step of 40 seconds, a ratio of 4.55 iterations in real time space to one iteration in Laplace space was obtained. The decrease in the number of iterations indicated that the sequential part of the simulator has been reduced. As a preliminary study, the results of the transform method were considered sufficiently successful to be extended to problems that are more nonlinear.
Awang, Mariyamni. (1991). Application of Parallel Programming to Reservoir Simulation. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/fm248ww8094
